schools.summary: Matthew Henry: Bildad twice began with a 'How long,' so Job answers with a 'How long' too; better cause to defend ourselves than to offend our brethren, yet disputation tempts men to magnify themselves.
Gill: Job heard Bildad out in silence, then rose in his own defence.
Clarke sketches the sweep of the reply — cruelty of friends, forsaking by kin and wife, the plea for pity, and the confession of hope.
Keil and Delitzsch justify the outburst as a well-earned 'quousque tandem'; Ellicott notes Job begins as Bildad had, provoked by an offensive and malicious speech.
Gill weighs which vexation is worst and finds it this — to be vexed to the heart by one's own friends.
Henry: the vexation of the soul is worse than of the bones; they came to comfort and set themselves to rob him of God, conscience, and good name.
Clarke: the friends are 'cold-blooded acquaintances,' not one touched with tenderness.

Clarke and Wesley take 'ten times' as many times (cf. Gen. 31:7), and 'make yourselves strange' as friends who knew him in prosperity now treating him as a stranger — circumstances change men's minds.
Gill: the number is round, not exact; to be reproached by friends as a hypocrite is the cutting thing.
Henry gathers the aggravations — reproached, unashamed, unblushing — yet owns that so exact a count of wrongs is itself peevish.
Gill: a concession, not a confession — good men may err, but Job's error stays with himself, not imposed on others.
Clarke: the supposed error hurt no one but Job himself; Wesley: if he sinned, he alone suffers and deserves pity, not reproach.
Henry ranks the errors of Job's judgment among things excusable — it is folly to think ourselves infallible, and a private error is self-punishing.
Gill catches the swagger — the friends look and talk big, resolve to run Job down, and magnify what they call his error.
Henry: they magnified themselves to depress him, a base thing to trample the down; and worst, they plead his reproach against his integrity, whereas Paul pleaded a good conscience (2 Cor. 1:12).
Clarke unfolds the 'net' by ancient combat — the Roman retiarius, the Persian noose, the Gothic hoop-net cast over horse or man.
Ellicott: Job answers Bildad's substance without his words — it is God who has taken him in his net (cf. Job 16:7; 13:27).
Gill: all Job's afflictions are from God's hand; 'perverted' not that God made him perverse, for God perverts no judgment.
Henry: it is barbarous to persecute whom God has smitten (Ps. 69:26) — let God's controversy end before the friends begin theirs.

themes: God the author of the ruin
tracing the stroke to God's hand

schools.summary: Gill takes 'wrong' as the violence done by Sabean, Chaldean, and Satan, cried against in open court yet unredressed.
Ellicott: the picture of a persecuted, forsaken, imprisoned man, his hope torn up like a tree (Job 14:7), enhances the coming confession.
Clarke: 'I complain of violence, but no one comes to my help'; Wesley: the cry is unto God, the wrong chiefly the oppression of his friends.
Henry: God may for a time turn away his ear, and the afflicted must be excused if they complain — woe unto us if God be against us.

themes: God seeming to turn away his ear

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch set the verse at the head of the strophe tracing stroke after stroke to God — the fenced way, darkened paths, stripped glory, uprooted hope.
Gill: God sometimes builds a wall of hewn stones across the pilgrim's road, so he stands still, not knowing what course to steer.
Clarke hears the language of the hunted beast hemmed in, or an army seizing all the passes.
Henry: Job looks forward for deliverance and finds it out of sight — 'darkness in my paths, and none to tell me how long' (Ps. 74:9).
Gill: not Job's spiritual glory or robe of righteousness, but his civil glory — wealth, family, house — stripped as from a plundered traveller, all ascribed to God.
Wesley: 'glory' is estate, children, authority; 'crown' all his power, his honour laid in the dust; Clarke: reduced so as to lose all honour and respect.
Henry: see the vanity of worldly glory — soon stripped, and whatever strips us, we must own God's hand in it.
Gill reads destruction on every side of estate and body alike, the removed hope like a tree dug about and its roots cut.
Clarke: no more hope of restoration than of a tree growing whose roots are torn out; Wesley: 'I am gone,' a lost man, yet the good man's hope is but transplanted to the garden of God.
Henry: reckoned undone for this world, hope removed like a felled tree — yet with good men only removed, from the sand to the rock, things temporal to eternal.
Clarke reads vv.7-13 as one sustained figure of a hostile invasion, this verse marking the point where the invader wastes all with fire and sword.
Gill: the metaphor turns to open warfare — Job imagines the fire of God's wrath kindled and set in battle-array, the mistaken apprehension of many a good man.
Ellicott anchors the language to Job's earlier cry of being torn as an enemy (Job 16:9).
Henry corrects the apprehension: whom God afflicts he does not treat as enemies — as many as he loves he chastens; it is the discipline of his sons.
Gill: the troops are Job's afflictions, God's soldiers at his command, that come and go at his word.
Wesley: the troops are afflictions marching under God's conduct; to 'raise up their way' is to cast up a siege-trench.
Henry gives the siege full shape — it grieved Job not that his miseries came in troops but that they were God's troops; once the hedge of Job 1:10, now a trench thrown up against him.

themes: the hedge turned to a siege
the same hand that guarded now assaults

schools.summary: Ellicott: human desertion is hardly less terrible than being forsaken by God, and the Psalmist copied the line (Ps. 88:8); the sorrow fits the Man of Sorrows. Keil and Delitzsch read a widening circle of desertion.
Gill keeps the war-figure: as war cuts an enemy off from his allies, God keeps far from Job all who might comfort him.
Wesley: eye the hand of God in the slights of friends as in the injuries of enemies.
Henry: God ordered the estrangement for Job's trial, though it was Satan that alienated their minds and their ingratitude is not excused.

themes: God's ordering hand in the slight

schools.summary: Gill: 'failed' not that they died but that they ceased to be near in affection — kinsfolk near in blood no longer near in heart.
Clarke: 'my kinsfolk have departed' — all left his house, now there is no hope of gain.
Henry: kinsfolk who claimed him in prosperity now fail him, familiar friends forget him — so uncertain is the friendship of men, but God fails not in need.

themes: God the friend who does not fail

schools.summary: Gill: those in the house are strangers and proselytes Job had sheltered in hospitality, now reckoning their benefactor a foreigner; he cites Jerome on Job's house at Carnea in Batanea.

Clarke: the contempt shown to the fallen from affluence — reverenced by all, now esteemed by none ('Bishop quondam'/'knave semper'); Wesley notes the maids, whose sex commonly has the more compassionate heart.
Henry: the master looks to be cared for by his own household, yet Job's worst foes were of his own house.

themes: the world's usage of the fallen

schools.summary: Gill: a trusty, favoured servant who owed ready obedience will not come at his afflicted master's call.
Keil and Delitzsch: the home-born slave who once saw every command in his master's eye now gives no answer; Job is obliged to entreat him.
Henry: Job, who did not despise his servant's cause (Job 31:13), now entreats where he might command, and is met with silence.

themes: the servant who will not answer

schools.summary: Gill weighs three senses of 'my breath is strange to my wife' — foul breath, or his disagreeable speech since he checked her counsel, or his very life grown wearisome to her.
Keil and Delitzsch take the confidential circle now turned away (the men of his counsel, even the three); Ellicott would rather render the clause of Job's kindness to his brethren.
Clarke: Job may adjure his wife by the children who sealed their love, perhaps hinting some yet remained, too young for the fatal feast.
Henry: because he would not curse God and die, his breath was strange to her too — the devil spared her to be his tormentor.
Gill: young children, taught by their parents' scorn, mock 'old Job with his boils'; profane mockers jeer at his religion and ask where his God is.
Wesley: 'I arose' — Job rose from his seat to show respect to these his inferiors, and for that courtesy they spoke against him.
Henry: the children born in his house despise him — when God withdraws a man's honour, even babes presume upon it.
Gill: 'the men of my secret,' bosom friends to whom Job opened his heart, now abhor the sight of him, and not one shows respect.
Ellicott glosses them the men of his counsel; Keil and Delitzsch note the deliberate movement inward, closing on the betrayal nearest the bone.
Wesley and Clarke: his inmost intimates and confidants, to whom he imparted all his thoughts, are turned against him.
Henry: those he loved were worse than publicans, not only turning from him but against him, to make him odious and justify their strangeness.

Clarke and Ellicott read 'escaped with the skin of my teeth' as a proverb of the narrowest escape — a hair's breadth from death; Ellicott owns the phrase is far from clear; Keil hears the voice growing feeble toward the coming entreaty.
Gill: flesh consumed by disease and grief, the bones sticking to the skin — Job a mere skeleton.
Henry: what little reason to indulge the body, which after all our care is consumed by the diseases it carries in its own seeds.

themes: escaped with the skin of the teeth

schools.summary: Henry begs the plea in language enough to break a heart of stone — if nothing else, be sorry for me, for the hand of God has touched me.
Keil and Delitzsch hear a new strain, the voice weaker, importunate, aimed at the friends' heart; Ellicott marks an exceeding great and bitter cry (cf. Job 16:20).
Gill: the doubled cry marks the vehemence of his distress and gently reproves the friends' want of pity.
Clarke: the iteration indicates the depth of his distress; Wesley: his spirit is touched with a sense of God's wrath, the most grievous of calamities.

themes: the plea for compassion not vindication
the hand of God touching him

schools.summary: Gill: God as sovereign may hunt a man with affliction and is accountable to none, but that is no warrant for the friends to join the chase.

Clarke: will ye persecute my soul while God persecutes my body? Wesley: 'as God' claims a divine knowledge and authority they have not, and, like beasts of prey, they are not satisfied to devour the flesh but must break the bones.

Ellicott refers the language to Job 16:9; Keil and Delitzsch, reading 'upon the dust' at v.25, already lay down that this speech expresses no hope of bodily recovery, rendering v.26 'without my flesh shall I behold Eloah.'
Henry: God's rebukes are enough; the friends need not add wormwood and gall — aim to be like the most merciful, not the most mighty.

themes: Keil's threshold reading of the confession

schools.summary: Henry finds no weightier lines in all the conferences — Job's appeal and cordial, spoken under an extraordinary impulse of the Spirit, after which his despairing passages cease (Heb. 11:14).

Clarke corrects 'printed' to 'traced out,' printing being unknown for two thousand years, and lists the writing-modes of Job's day; Wesley marks that God granted the wish — the words are written in his book.
Ellicott: these three verses are more emphatic than any Job has spoken, and 'now' = here points to the confession at hand.
Gill: the words Job would have recorded are those he is about to speak — his faith in a living Redeemer and the resurrection.
Gill: the iron stile on a sheet of lead, or letters cut in stone and filled with molten lead, as ancient monuments were made for permanence.

Clarke reports the chisel-and-lead method but prefers taking Job to name the several writing-modes of his day (Pliny, Pausanias); Wesley: they graved letters in stone and filled the cuts with lead to make them plain.
Gill argues the 'goel' can be neither a mere man (who could not 'live' and 'stand at the latter day') nor God the Father, but only Christ the Son, the near kinsman of Lev. 25:25.
Henry: Christ the living Redeemer, the near kinsman who redeems the mortgaged inheritance; Job, stripped of all, still says 'my Redeemer.'
Wesley: the 'goel' most fitly agrees to Christ, our nearest kinsman; Clarke, weighing resurrection vs. temporal restoration, comes down for a prophecy of redemption by Christ.

Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch read the Redeemer as God himself, the eternal Vindicator ('faith in the I am'); Ellicott takes 'upon dust' literally (cf. Job 41:33), against 'over my dust'; Keil renders 'as the last One will He arise from the dust,' denying a hope of bodily recovery.

debates.question: Who is the 'redeemer' (goel) whom Job knows to live?

sides.position: the incarnate Christ, the near kinsman who shall stand at the latter day
God himself, the eternal living Vindicator who takes on the goel's functions, not named as Christ
a mere mortal vindicator who should rise to plead his cause (named and rejected)

debates.question: Does the passage foretell resurrection and redemption by Christ, or Job's temporal restoration in this life?

sides.position: a future resurrection and redemption by Christ
Job's restoration to health and prosperity in this life

debates.question: How is 'at the latter day upon the earth' (al-aphar) to be rendered?

sides.position: at the end of time, standing over the earth to raise the dead — a resurrection scene
'upon the dust' / 'arise from the dust,' standing last after all pass away, no bodily-recovery hope

schools.summary: Gill: after skin, worms, and grave have utterly consumed his body, he is yet assured he shall rise — 'in my flesh' a bodily resurrection.
Clarke: 'I shall arise from the dead, have a renewed body, and see him with eyes of flesh'; Wesley: with bodily eyes, his flesh raised and reunited to his soul, in the beatifying vision.
Henry: soul and body come together again, the same body raised a glorious and spiritual body (1 Cor. 15:44); this is the redemption of the soul from the grave (Ps. 49:15), not temporal deliverance.

Keil and Delitzsch construe 'min' as privative — 'without my flesh shall I behold Eloah,' a spirit beholding God, no bodily recovery; Ellicott holds 'from my flesh' in balance — present faith amid decay, or something yet to come.

debates.question: Does 'min-basari' mean 'in my flesh' or 'without my flesh'?

sides.position: 'in my flesh' — a bodily resurrection, seeing God in a risen, glorified body
'without / apart from my flesh' — the disembodied spirit beholding God, no bodily-recovery hope
'from my flesh' left ambiguous — either present faith amid corruption or a future sight

themes: 'in my flesh shall I see God'
min-basari — in or without the flesh
the destruction of the flesh as its threshold

schools.summary: Clarke fixes 'not another' (zar, not a stranger) as the redeeming Kinsman, Job's personal interest in the resurrection; Wesley: with these self-same eyes, in this same body, a sight most sweet to repeat.
Gill: a seeing all Job's own, for his pleasure and inexpressible joy.

Ellicott: the words may not teach the resurrection directly, but express the faith of which it is the only natural justification, so that the confession heads the Christian burial office; Keil renders 'my veins languish in my bosom,' the frailty returning even as the hope soars.
Henry: Job's whole desire summed up in this — let me have this, and I have nothing more to desire (1 John 3:2; Rev. 21:3).

debates.question: How far do these words teach the resurrection of the flesh?

sides.position: a direct confession — Job's own risen eyes shall behold God, and not another
not directly, but the firm conviction of the faith of which resurrection is the only natural justification
a vision of God with reins languishing, guarded as to bodily recovery

themes: the reach of the resurrection hope
the confession at the head of the burial office

schools.summary: Gill: Job directs his friends to the use they should make of his creed — to own the root of true religion found in him and cease their persecuting.
Clarke hears a coming repentance ('how did we persecute him!') and notes over a hundred MSS. read 'in him'; Wesley: the 'root' is a root of true religion, which is a living faith.

Ellicott prefers 'why should He persecute any man without cause? and therefore the root of the matter (the cause of the affliction) must be found in me' — the friends' cruel logic, not their repentance.
Henry: see that the root of the matter — grace in the heart, love, faith, hatred of sin — be in us; many have it who differ from us, and we persecute such at our peril.

debates.question: What is 'the root of the matter,' and does the clause voice the friends' repentance or their cruel logic?

sides.position: the essence of true piety / religion found in Job — a call to the friends' repentance
the cause of the affliction, which the friends reason must lie in Job — their persecuting logic

schools.summary: Gill: the sword is avenging divine justice, lest God whet it to avenge the wrongs of the innocent.

Clarke: such anger God will punish, and the inequities of this life prove a future judgment; he also reports and weighs Kennicott's third view; Wesley reads the sword as a coming judgment and the whole as timely admonition.
Henry: a word of terror to those found smiting their fellow-servant (Matt. 24:49), especially from the sin of rashly judging brethren (Matt. 7:1; Jam. 3:1).

outliers.note: Proposes a third reading of the whole confession — neither resurrection after death nor temporal prosperity, but a divine conviction that God would appear before Job's death to vindicate his integrity in this life ('my Vindicator liveth... he shall arise over this dust'). Clarke reports it fairly but judges the theory better than its arguments and the version more than the Hebrew will bear, holding still to the resurrection reading.
